editorial.headline: Furniture Retail: Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Furniture retail is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent risk-based PMA moratorium blocks registration there.
editorial.body:
Furniture retail, in this record, means the retail sale of furnishing items: tables, chairs, wardrobes, beds, bookcases, shoe racks, buffets, mattresses and mattress bed frames. The scope is product-led and concrete, covering the pieces through which rooms are furnished rather than reducing the trade to a single product line. Storage and display furniture sit beside sleeping furniture, so the activity holds together a broad but intelligible retail offer. Its centre of gravity is the sale of furniture itself, as the listed examples consistently make clear. Each item gives the category a recognisable commercial boundary.

The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises. That full spread is not a throwaway classification detail: those are the business scales expressly available for the activity, from Mikro through Besar. It says nothing about a preference among them; each is named in the stated availability. The breadth of that eligibility situates furniture retail as an activity open across the recorded scale spectrum, while leaving the PMA question to the national and local rules given separately. For founders, that scale field answers the availability question—not foreign ownership or Bali’s local PMA decision.

Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA—open—and the recorded maximum foreign ownership is 100%. Put plainly, the national ceiling permits full foreign ownership of this activity. The source cited for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This is a clear starting point for reading the code, yet it cannot be read as an automatic Bali outcome. The slim record presents national ownership and Bali PMA registration as distinct parts of the same compliance picture. The 100% figure is a ceiling, not a Bali registration approval.

In Bali, the conclusion changes decisively. The status is Blocked (risk class), and the record marks PMA registration blocked. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low on every scope. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium—recorded in May 2026—blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. The result is direct and should not be softened: a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today, even with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The Bali rule is sourced to Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP.
